comments.author: gertlabs
comments.textZhHtml:
We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon in 100 unsaturated, competitive and cooperative coding environments. It's roughly in between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 in our testing, so it's maybe 2 months behind the frontier.

Google's major releases have usually done pretty well on our benchmarks because they're good at hard problems and open-ended decision making (with a well specified prompt), which obviously doesn't always translate to user experience. In particular, older Google models struggled to work efficiently in a harness. They seem to have solved that with Argon.

We did see a new problem which I hope they can fix. This is the first near-frontier model we've caught in infinite reasoning loops in a long time. We also saw a few examples of it failing to properly delineate reasoning blocks, so it has a higher failure rate than its competitors.

My overall impression is that Argon is a near-frontier model for engineering design, code analysis, and chat. It definitely has the intelligence to be a competitive coding assistant product, but a good coding assistant needs to be polished, so I hope they can clean up the CoT bugs.

Data at https://gertlabs.com/rankings

comments.textZhHtml: At this point I'm interested less in how well a model can code, but more in how well it can produce code that humans can understand.

comments.author: booty
comments.textZhHtml:
I have had pretty decent success instructing OpenAI/Anthropic models to do this. By default, they don't care too much about human readability (which is understandable) but they're amenable to instruction.

- Basic style/linter rules (so you don't get 200-line functions, etc) paired w/ instructing your agent how to use them goes a long way (e.g., a sane rubocop.yml in your repo, plus a note in AGENTS.md telling the agents how to run rubocop, or whatever makes sense for your language) - I have a code review skill that specifically calls out human-readability concerns such as making sure that identifier names represent their contents and intended use

The other key IME is that you need to make readability/refactoring passes outside of a particular pull request. When working on a specific branch the LLMs will be somewhat myopic, and do stuff that looks pretty good in isolation, but when you zoom out and look at the bigger picture it's kind of a mess - for example, often they'll duplicate some code that existed elsewhere.

The LLMs are also pretty good at generating Mermaid charts and tracing execution flows, which is a great way to understand code. It doesn't help them to produce more readable code but it helps me to understand code I'm unfamiliar with.

comments.textZhHtml: I agree, and I find it sad that so many people and companies are in a rush to take the human out of the loop. But for agentic/human hybrids not even all of those work out well - and the error modes have more to do with the "alignment" of the human. That is, humans with strong knowledge, an aesthetic sense for structure, strong curiosity - those humans do well in this loop. Humans that just want to "make money" using the LLM as a slave, interacting with it as little as possible, taking no interest in what it does (bad company leadership in miniature) get poor outputs. When the human is an invested, knowledgeable curator of code, someone who has a vision that goes beyond the external, you get some really great stuff.

stories.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
stories.author: Philpax
summaryZh: Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion.At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.Growing our monorepoBefore we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?Principles for agent-scale source controlWith agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling,2 so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.How Scion worksIt’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.Data structuresIn Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.The shape of a changeset in Scion.This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.Scaling ScionA small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.Scion’s checkout architecture.Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.What we learned building ScionWe started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026.What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future.Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code.We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day.Observed performance improvements on native Scion repos.We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes.A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them.Contributing to the wider ecosystemWe see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case.Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities.Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful.However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well.Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential.AcknowledgementsWritten by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique.FootnotesStoring changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo.Specifically, the server component of Sapling, Mononoke. It pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion, in particular the Bonsai data model.

stories.title: Things to know when you get cancer
stories.titleZh: 患癌症时需要了解的事情
stories.author: jjmaxwell4
summaryZh: index Back to top 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.

You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.

comments.author: stochastician
comments.textZhHtml:
第二意见建议很棒，我告诉每个我认识的患有癌症的人。

我的妈妈于 2006 年在爱达荷州被诊断出患有 1 期癌症。当时我是麻省理工学院的一名博士生，实验室的一位朋友帮助我在丹娜—法伯癌症研究所获得了预约。我认为这可能有点过分了（这是一种常见的癌症），但我们还是这么做了。他们说爱达荷州的一切都是标准护理，但建议进行一项额外的测试，爱达荷州团队随后不情愿地进行了这项测试，结果发现了远处转移（第四阶段！），极大地改变了她的治疗轨迹。她又活了 15 年（妈妈，我想你）。

寻求第二意见很糟糕。我们中的许多人从出生起就注定要信任我们的临床医生。但你即将踏上旅程，而你的生命（或你所爱之人的生命）正处于危险之中。保险通常会涵盖它。你的医生不会被冒犯。

这样想：如果你正在向火星探测器部署代码，而你的同事要求在你按下 go 之前进行代码审查，你会被冒犯吗？这比那更重要。

第二种观点是我一路走来学到的东西。 在您根据初步诊断制定治疗计划之前获取它。 对于我妻子的卵巢癌，我们从克利夫兰诊所和 MSK 得到了两份第二意见（一份针对她的第一次诊断，一份针对她的复发），在这两种情况下，医生都不会建议/推翻原来医生的治疗计划。

他们完全没有手术，浪费时间。 今天面对同样的情况，我会简单地谎报是否制定了治疗计划。

第二条建议是尽最大努力进入临床试验，了解不合格治疗的情况。 例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

最后，我向身处困境的亲人伴侣推荐的一件事是，不要因试图“拯救患者”而分心，从而错过在此过程中与他们保持联系的机会。 拯救他们的生命不是你的责任，尽管当你身处其中时可能会有这种感觉。

comments.textZhHtml:
（我在癌症中心治疗患者，但意见是我自己的，而不是我雇主的。）

我完全鼓励任何想要其他意见的患者获得一个意见。如果可以在不无故拖延的情况下完成，那么在开始治疗计划之前就寻求一个绝对是非常好的建议。我想到规划癌症治疗就像排队登机：有些计划即使不完美，如果已经付诸实施，改变计划也比继续执行更危险。谢天谢地，很少有时候，我们在诊断或治疗上完全没有达成一致，最好在第一次治疗之前就解决好这一切。

但是，第二个意见并不只是因为它与最初的计划一致而浪费。根据我的经验，这实际上是最常见的结果，而且我认为，如果第二意见能够让您的原始团队按照规定做所有事情，这确实是一件好事。对于许多常见癌症，人们就最合适的一线治疗达成了共识，因为有经过同行评审的证据，并就如何应用这些证据达成了一致。当所有这些都指向有效的治疗，直至标准化的剂量和时间表，这确实是一件好事！

当对于不同综合癌症中心使用的（例如）两种合理方法中哪一种最好没有达成明确共识时，就会出现一些微妙之处。如果您查看指南，这两种方法都会被列为适当的，但可能会建议患者在 A 中心采用一种计划，在 B 中心采用不同的计划。

可以归结为，A 中心提供的治疗 A 与 B 提供的治疗结果相当。在这种情况下，如果患者住在 A 中心附近的街道上，并长途跋涉数百英里来 B 中心寻求第二意见，我几乎总是同意在 A 中心接受治疗 A。不是因为我试图管理哪个中心A 会想到我，但因为我真的相信这符合特定患者的最大利益。首先，在其他条件相同的情况下，我没有理由认为长途跋涉数百英里到 B 中心接受治疗会比留在当地更好。其次，总的来说，我强烈怀疑在 A 中心接受治疗 B（这不是他们最有经验的计划）会优于在 A 中心接受治疗 A。

而且，是的，我绝对建议患者在适当的时候将护理转移到我们的中心，并且我还建议患者在适当的时候离开我们的中心去其他地方（例如，为了一个特别有前途的临床试验选择）。我看到我的每一位同事都毫不犹豫地这样做。

当然，这只是从一个人的角度来看。我知道患者和家属可以从不同且完全有效的角度出发。但总而言之，请不要担心管理医生获得第二意见的情绪，并找到一个可以让您确信向您提供第二意见的人也不会考虑管理医生情绪的地方。希望他们能赢得您的信任，即一致意见意味着他们确实认为您的原始团队已经制定了最适合您的计划。

I can’t believe nobody’s brought this up yet, but the HomeView fundementally exists for one reason: to be a Matter hub for smarthome stuff. No iPad – or any portable Apple device - can be configured as a home hub for managing Matter-protocol devices. There’s no significant advantage to a HomeView over an iPad if you don’t have any Matter devices.

That’s why this device has multi-user support: you’re only supposed to have one of them, which everyone uses. The Apple TV also has good multi-user support, because Apple doesn’t expect you to connect one Apple TV per user to your television.

stories.title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet

stories.author: sighborg
summaryZh: Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition. But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...💙 AmandaLast week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over: the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.In a nutshell, here's what's happening:

This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.Let's get into it.Amazon charges sellers a lot of feesAmazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales. But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.

comments.author: steveBK123
comments.textZhHtml:
我发现 20 年前我在亚马逊购物是因为价格低廉，但 2020 年代以后我在亚马逊购物是因为他们的物流。

其他人的问题不仅仅是亚马逊发货速度快，我什至几乎不关心这一点。 问题是亚马逊按照可靠的预测时间表发货和交付。 当我点击亚马逊上的一件商品时，它说“周二到货”，那么有 95/100 次是这样。 我在可以做类似操作的特定竞争对手（B&H、Sweetwater 等）处购物。

到 2026 年，许多大大小小的在线商店仍然需要几天时间才能发送发货信息，然后使用错过预计到达时间的不可靠承运商。

我什至可以接受这些商店给出的狭窄范围或概率“90% 的时间在周二和周三之间到达”。 2-10 天，对于该范围的哪一端还不太清楚。

前几天，我不得不打包一件不是从亚马逊购买的产品，然后在一些奇怪的营业时间开车 25 分钟到特定公司的投递点...

stories.title: Passkeys are not a trap
stories.author: speckx
summaryZh: A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords.The ArgumentThe post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey.The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif>It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works...Your Passkeys Don't AttestThe passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none. I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone. If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now.Attestation Isn't What You Think It IsThe post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true.When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID, with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is.The YubiKey RecommendationThis is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation".YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!TOTP Is a Step BackwardsThe post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt. Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it. This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com. There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade...What You Should DoKeep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.SourcesI have some experience in this area:I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web. I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company.We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed.I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website.I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work.I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use.I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations. I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys.I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap. comments.author: chaboud
comments.textZhHtml:
我认为“密钥是一个陷阱”将是关于这个可用性噩梦的。有些网站一旦通过密钥连接，就几乎不可能以其他方式连接。有些支持多个密钥。有些则不然。 有些支持密钥或其他东西。有些则不然。

到目前为止，大约有 30% 的网站搞砸了......

comments.author: gortok
comments.textZhHtml:
这就是问题所在。

如果我不确定密钥能否像我的密码管理器和身份验证器应用程序一样工作（也就是说 100% 成功），我就不能采用密钥。

当我说“密钥是一个陷阱”时，它们是一个可用性陷阱，没有人可以肯定地证明我不会因为我决定采用密钥而在痛苦的情况中醒来。

comments.author: jasomill
comments.textZhHtml:
具有讽刺意味的是，万能钥匙最适合与在所有用户设备上同步万能钥匙的密码管理器结合使用，但这也是它们相对于传统密码的安全优势最小的情况。

comments.author: solyin

comments.author: Dylan16807

是的，但是如果您有一个设置良好的密码管理器，您将永远不会首先复制粘贴密码。 如果密码没有显示，您就知道存在问题。

comments.author: thayne
comments.textZhHtml: 如果网站始终正确地注释输入，则情况确实如此，但事实并非如此。因此，密码管理器只能猜测输入的用户名、密码等，但他们并不总是能猜对。

comments.author: nh2
comments.textZhHtml:
> 对于技术愚蠢的人

> 密码不显示，你知道有问题

这就是你的矛盾。

普通人只会假设今天某些技术又不起作用了。

万能钥匙的一个关键点似乎是它向网站所有者保证用户不会被网络钓鱼，而不必假设用户是否是网络钓鱼的技术愚蠢。

comments.author: Brian_K_White
comments.textZhHtml:
“它向网站所有者保证用户不会被网络钓鱼”

好吧，这对网站所有者来说多好。

问题是我的首要任务是我绝对有能力永远不会通过我无法控制的某种方式失去我最重要的资产，而不是网站的便利性。

在银行、商店甚至政府都在一英里外设有办公桌的日子里，使用不完善的系统是可以的。亲自去清理一切并覆盖所有可能的“通常是这样的”，用你的身体在场，驾驶执照和出生证明，或者只是五个人都证明他们认识你。

我们不再有那个最终的后备计划，所以任何人都试图证明基本上欺骗人们做一些不明智的事情，这实际上使他们面临更大的风险，因为他们的生活不太受自己的控制，并且在声称关心用户的旗帜下这样做安全！

太棒了。

comments.author: trinsic2
comments.textZhHtml: 这对我来说是个难题。密钥实际上是为了保护站点而不是用户。恕我直言，它的设计确实是向后的。

comments.author: Dylan16807
comments.textZhHtml: 我不知道他们是否知道如何从管理器中复制密码...

comments.author: kergonath
comments.textZhHtml: 它们必须如此，因为密码管理器经常无法正确检测用户名或密码字段，在这种情况下您必须手动复制和粘贴。

comments.author: Dylan16807
comments.textZhHtml:
我遇到这种情况的次数比网站被破坏的次数还要少。 如果我无法复制粘贴，那就没问题了。

如果有人只从浏览器 UI 保存密码，他们真的不知道如何手动复制密码，同时相处得很好。

comments.author: vel0city
comments.textZhHtml:
几十年来我使用过许多密码管理器。由于糟糕/恶意的网站设计，需要对尚未配置插件的浏览器/应用程序进行身份验证，检测正确站点的插件存在错误等，我仍然不得不时不时地复制和粘贴密码。最后，如果用户可以将其复制并粘贴到任何地方，那么用户将将其复制并粘贴到任何地方。

同时还有其他安全优势。使用密码时，该静态凭证将在握手中传输。它可能会在两者之间的某个地方处理不当，现在整个根凭证可能会受到损害。这对于密钥来说是不可能的。凭证永远不会离开客户。在一些实现中，凭证永远不会离开安全飞地，甚至永远不会进入客户端的系统内存。对于密码，你不能说同样的话，甚至不是很接近。

comments.author: fiddlerwoaroof
comments.textZhHtml: 是的，现在很多网站似乎在我真正想要的地方阻止或搞乱了自动填充：我无法说出有多少网站破坏了信用卡自动完成、TOTP 代码自动完成（例如通过 Apple 的本机 TOTP 实现）、用户名/密码自动完成。我永远无法真正判断这是无能还是错误的安全观念，但这非常烦人。

comments.author: kccqzy
comments.textZhHtml:
> 我确实很欣赏密钥的采用带来了对硬件安全令牌的更广泛支持

根据我的经验，这根本没有发生。许多站点支持密钥，但仅支持当前设备上存储的本机密钥，而不支持硬件安全密钥。许多网站甚至不允许使用多个万能钥匙，坦率地说，如果您使用硬件安全性，这是必需的，因为您将需要多个硬件，以防其中一个丢失。

comments.author: rlpb
comments.textZhHtml:
> 许多网站支持密钥，但仅支持当前设备上存储的本机密钥，而不是硬件安全密钥。

这是浏览器的功能，而不是网站的功能。

不过，您关于多个密钥的观点是有效的。这也影响着我。我使用多个硬件密钥，但因此无法注册许多站点。

comments.author: nine_k
comments.textZhHtml:
> 在用户的所有设备上同步它们

从技术上讲可以从创建它的设备上泄露的密钥有什么意义？我认为万能钥匙的整个前提是它们无法被复制，因此可以像设备访问控制一样值得信任。我错过了什么吗？

comments.author: xp84
comments.textZhHtml:
让它们真正卡在设备上（例如锁定在安全区域内）会带来不同的可用性问题。主要是您必须在每台设备上为每个网站重新进行设置。买新手机？回到石器时代。在新设备上使用每个站点的密码进行身份验证，找到“添加密钥”位置，然后安装它。

stories.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
stories.titleZh: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
stories.author: layer8
summaryZh: In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does. Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs. One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful: it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its answers matter. An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse. Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not? The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful. Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does. What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any. I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment. The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

comments.author: jgord
comments.textZhHtml:
Its probable that AI will roll out much faster than humans can develop that skill of using it in a way that increases not decreases human knowledge over time.

The current slew of excellent LLMs will probably cause a decades long dip in human cognitive ability.

If social media on smartphones had an impact of ability of students to concentrate, LLM AI will likely have a much greater negative impact on education.

There are trillions of dollars of investment pushing for humans to trust whatever an LLM says, and very little money behind encouraging people to tackle hard problems themselves and train themselves to think.

I have to say honestly, that AI looks like an apocalypse for human thinking [ Im glad Tao is warning people, I just dont think many people will listen ]

comments.author: Stevvo
comments.textZhHtml: I've learnt more since the advent of LLMs than I did in the 10 years prior. And it's not just me; that is most people's experience with LLMs. But most of those people would also concur with your apocalyptic thinking. AI is the apocalypse for thinking, except for me, only I am smart enough and experienced enough to maintain my cognitive ability while using LLMs.

comments.author: 0x696C6961
comments.textZhHtml: The problem is that if you take away the LLM, all of a sudden you can't do any of the things you "learned". It's confusing familiarity with understanding.

comments.author: indoordin0saur
comments.textZhHtml:
I did actually use an LLM to teach myself photoshop recently for a fantasy map building project. Mostly I'd just ask it things like "I have a mask with 50/50 gray and would like an elevation height map to be an embossed layer on it. Where do I find that in the menus?" those sorts of questions.

I finished the project out feeling pretty confident in my photoshop abilities. Then I did a similar project later and realized I had to open up the LLM again as there were still a ton of holes in my knowledge. After this second time though I'm feeling confident enough on my own that referring back to the LLM is increasingly less common, as it's just a waste of time if I already know what to do.

comments.author: skeeter2020
comments.textZhHtml: but this is not how people use - or providers sell - LLMs. They don't ask questions about how to do small steps, they just ask it to do the entire project, finish quickly and learn nothing. If the workflow was many, tight iterations it would be closer to a tool than an automation.

comments.author: drdeca
comments.textZhHtml: Clearly some people use it in this sort of “how to do this small step” way.

comments.author: johnnyanmac
comments.textZhHtml:
"some" do not a system make. "Some" people succeed in the current educational system, but others would argue people succeed "despite" the system, not "because" of it.

It seems we're about to get a massive stress test of such a theory.

comments.author: semiquaver
comments.textZhHtml:
Says who?

Sounds like you’re attacking a strawman

comments.author: rtsang1
comments.textZhHtml:
It sounds like a fair criticism.

LLM is an issue (to most of us) when it replaces exploration, thinking and effort to aquire skill. Whether it's vibe-coding an app, or thinking through a math problem. Jury is out this will atually dimish the next generation of thinkers. But seems like a valid concern to me.

2. This particular case of LLM usage (to teach us photoshop) is replacing traditional tutorials. It can help people learn things. This is also valid to me.

The existence of 2, doesn't eliminate 1. Existence of 1 doesn't eliminate 2. There's no strawmans here. I also think it's fair that the promise of LLMs (and AIs), isn't to replace tutorials, but to displace and automate much more.

comments.author: Folcon
comments.textZhHtml:
As someone who spent a lot of time supporting users and understanding their challenges with these tools, there's a lot of can you do X vs how can I do X, at least a 10x if not 100x difference.

IE: Model do this for me vs teach me.

Enough that I know people who have built businesses purely training people.

comments.author: johnnyanmac
comments.textZhHtml:
Statistics on cheating in schools and interviews?

The paradigm shift on how every medium+ size FOSSS repo needs to take in PR submission?

The increase in bot activity in social media/

Who's the ones saying this is actually creating higher quality products? No one talks about quality anymore: only speed.

comments.author: Tanjreeve
comments.textZhHtml: Look at the marketing. "Complete projects", "Build apps". "Get advice". How often are we seeing "build a functioning workflow and validation pipeline and collaborate in incremental stages" or anything boring to that effect?

comments.author: Yizahi
comments.textZhHtml: Anthropic themselves?

comments.author: joquarky
comments.textZhHtml: How dug in are you on this perception?

comments.author: johnnyanmac
comments.textZhHtml:
Based on my experiences seeing what people actually do with AI tools: very. If this was a situation where I was seeing higher quality apps, PR's, and community building I would have few qualms about AI.

Instead it's created swamps in the art community, choas and bloat in the FOSS communities, a stronger sense of mistrust with traditional search, a deepening of the Dead Internet Theory, more broken tools to scrounge through... where is this supposed "benefit" I'm getting out of this?

comments.author: gridspy
comments.textZhHtml: Bear in mind it takes very few individuals to create a LOT of this sort of low-quality AI content. That makes it hard to judge how many are using Agentic methods vs "only Advice" vs "no AI."

comments.author: foobarbecue
comments.textZhHtml:
There was a brief moment where programs had decent built-in help you could search to easily find where stuff was in menus. Didn't need a billion parameters or a giant faraway data center...

Or, better, the global menu search. Intellij's shift+shift shortcut is great.

comments.author: Diti
comments.textZhHtml: This knowledge has always been present in the product’s documentation. What you needed for learning is a chatbot, not general-purpose probabilistic automation which acts as a conversation simulator.

comments.author: springtimesun
comments.textZhHtml:
LLMs have also pushed me to learn a lot, but I don’t find the shape to be terribly different than before. I rarely remember the exact sequence of commands or flags or syntax. What my learning was useful for before and after LLMs is to 1) build an intuition of how something behaves and what it should do and 2) expose me to non-obvious possibilities that I wouldn’t have come to on my own. With those two things in place, the next execution without the LLM is a docs search, same as it always was (for me maybe some people are better at remembering this stuff).

What’s different after LLMs for me is that there are some things that just don’t care about and I’m fine if they are a black box that the agent handles for me. I didn’t have that luxury before.

stories.title: The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
stories.titleZh: 英国人均发电量低于 20 世纪 70 年代
stories.author: karakoram
summaryZh: Data InsightsElectricity generation per person in the United Kingdom has fallen by a third from its early-2000s peakOctober 03, 2026Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.Explore how electricity generation has changed in your own countryOur latest Data InsightsSee all Data Insights TodayA long-term perspective on humanity’s battle against malariaMax RoserAccording to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000.The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000.Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible.Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress.If you want to be a part of this historic change, read my brief article on how you can contribute to humanity’s battle against malariaOctober 13China reduced extreme poverty fast, but Indonesia hasn’t been far behindHannah Ritchie and Pablo ArriagadaChina is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong: many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines.Explore progress against poverty across the world in our data explorerOctober 10What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean?Hannah RitchieMany of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:A) Less than 1%B) Less than 36%C) Less than 66%Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.Read my article, which looks at this question in more detailOctober 8The new Living Planet Index reports a 73% average decline in studied wildlife populationsHannah RitchieThe new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.But it tells us none of that.It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.As I explained in a previous article, being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.Read my explainer on what the Living Planet Index captures, and what’s different in this report from previous onesOctober 6Child mortality has declined in all world regionsMax RoserIn 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.Explore child mortality data for every country in our interactive data explorerOctober 1Europe is older, but Latin America is aging fasterEsteban Ortiz-OspinaThe median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. 只有当您有足够的白光以确保下一小时内您想看到的所有物体都被完全照亮时，白光才有用。 如果有任何例外，那么您不应该使用白色精简版。
